description.narrative:
CICADA's mission is to see a thriving, diverse, empowered CCI that contributes to the flourishing Cambodian. CICADA’s missions are to impact national policies through leading research, capacity building and foster dialogue to mobilize the development andgrowth ofthe CCIs for national and global recognition of Cambodian arts, culture and creativity. Our key stakeholders are artists and cultural workers, who include youth, women, indigenous people and people with disabilities. Problem: Representation gapand knowledge gap regarding policy
CICADA's research shows that 90% of cultural workers—particularly in rural areas—work without formal contracts, leaving them vulnerable to exploitation and without recourse. Less than 10% are affiliated with civil society organizations, NGOs, or government bodies, creating a representation gap that excludes them from policy processes affecting their livelihoods. This lack of organization undermines their ability to advocate collectively for better working conditions,fair compensation, and social protections. From CICADA’s observation from conducting 20 training workshops for 400 cultural workers in various provinces, mostly they are not aware about Cambodia's National Policy for Culture, let alone how the budget worksnor have they received any report about financial expenditure on culture.
With 74.4% having only basic education and 90% lacking organizational representation, rural cultural workers are systematically excluded from both economic advancement and democratic participation. CCI workers are not aware of the budgetprocess - how is it decided or allocated or monitored. From CICADA’s regular consultations with CCI workers, we observe that they often are told by their respective provincial Department of Cultures that there is no budget for artistic or cultural activities. However, there has never been any public disclosure or discussion openly. From CICADA’s research in 2022 which revealed that CCI workers do not feel confident in engaging in policy development. This proves that having the courage to ask, make an official request, or advocate for budget transparency is not in sight. Without this knowledge we cannot advocate for necessary investment into CCIs. The organisations that serve these communitiesgetno public funding and no knowledge in order to advocate. When it comes to cultural CSOs, particularly those serving independent artists including Cambodian Living Arts, Bophana Center, Phare Ponleu Selpak and Epic Arts,there is also a major knowledgegap with respect to public finances. While these CSOs (all members of CICADA) regularly work to lobby the government on matters of cultural policy, they never engage in dialogue about budget - having no access to public funding and becoming accustomed tosourcing financing from other sources. In order to complement and support any awareness raising and training among independent workers, it is essential to do a robust capacity-building program among these organisations - who between them serve youth, indigenous and disabled artists across the country.
Although this project targets artists and cultural workers, more or less this project might be beneficial to some provincial Departments of Culture as well. Through our work these past years, it has become apattern that many provincial departments of culture staff are also practicing their arts outside of their work.
Problem: Lack of investment into the CCIs
There is also a lack of investment from the Royal Government of Cambodia into the culturaland creative industries. Since 2018, the National Budget allocation for the Ministry of Culture and Fine Arts (MoCFA) has seen a steady decline (2018: USD 47.53m, 2020: USD 46.29m, 2022: USD 39.52m). This decrease of national attention on arts and culture is further worsened by more than half (estimated as the ministerial budget is not public) of the annual budget being earmarked for heritage activities related to the Angkor Archaeological Park. The ADB Institute in its recent report Creative Economy 2030: Imagining and Delivering a Robust, Creative, Inclusive, and Sustainable Recovery, identifies Cambodia as among the ‘least ready’ in ASEAN to develop its entertainment industry, due to “insufficient attention to this industry from the government”. Opportunity: Creative Economy a hot-topic in Cambodia, and a strong potential employer of youth, women and people with disabilities
Globally, the Creative Economy is the largestemployer of young people [15-29] versus any other sector, and approximately half ofits workers are women. Overall, it is an inclusive sector and presents an opportunity, however in Cambodia this sector is not yet well recognised or invested in. Thus, works toward advocacy for more public funding on the CCI sectors prove necessary. This though needs to come with capacity building for the young cultural workers to understand the creative economy, its benefits and factors to contribute its sustainability, which again investment would bring more job opportunity for them in return.
Lately, it is observed that the Royal Government of Cambodia is interested in the creative economy. In June 2025, the Ministry of Culture and Fine Arts with the support of UNESCO Cambodia conducted a consultation on ‘Shaping the Future: Toward a NationalPolicy for Cambodia’s Cultural and Creative Industries’. Similarly, Cambodia had recently hosted the Mekong Forum: Harnessing Inclusive and Resilient GMS through New Economies where creative economy is one of the key themes of the forum. However, thereisno strategic plan and no budget allocated for it. In addition, CICADA finds that there are 19ministries and national councils that are supporting the creative industries in silo without any clear governance structure. Thus, it is time for CICADA to playa lobbying role in connecting major players in both governmental ministries such as Ministry of Cultureand Fine Arts, Ministry of Industry, Science, Technology, and Innovation, Ministry of Tourism, Ministry of Economy and Finance and private sectors to discuss the governance infrastructure and advocate for financial investment and transparent expenditure.
As mentioned above, the creative industries budget comes from diverse ministries as it is managed by diverse ministries. There is no central coordination or visibility. Work towards a CCI budget at national level can also be explored to see how open and possible it is.
In sum, it is useful to combine the existing curriculum of My Arts and Culture, My Rights and Introduction to Cambodia's CulturalPolicy with a concentration on creative economy, and its financial nature and advocacy tool to train key cultural based organizations who are members of CICADA and artists and cultural workers will be beneficial. In addition, it is important to build a stronger ally with leading cultural CSOs where they can represent their own community and could become advocates for PFM with CICADA and other stakeholders. In consequence, after such trainings, CICADA shall grow a knowledgeable CCI sector who are readyto have insights about the creative industries and could support advocacy initiatives toward transparent budget for cultural and creative sector.

participating-org.narrative:
CICADA is the Creative Industries of Cambodia Association for Development and Advocacy, co-founded in 2020 by six leaders from cultural organisations, and formally registered since 2022. In its role as representative and advocate for the cultural and creative industries (CCI), CICADA seeks to strengthen the role civil society plays in policymaking for a sustainable and inclusive infrastructure and to ensure that the sector is at the heart of political, economic, and social decision-making. Through providing civic education and access to information on the cultural policy landscape, it empowers cultural and creative workers to assume their democratic rights to participate in policymaking that impact their livelihoods and the country’s access to the economic, social and environmental benefits of culture, and to hold decision makers and law enforcement accountable. CICADA is a membership association and currentlyhas 152 members representing eight sectors from 7 provinces dominantly from Battambang, Siem Reap, and Phnom Penh.
What is unique about CICADA is that CICADA is the only institution that works on policy advocacy in cultural and creative industries. It was established by six cultural leaders who represent six arts and cultural organisations. They have been working and serving the sectors for decades. With their passion and wish to see inclusive and supportive policy development for the CCI sector, CICADA exists and has been serving, representing, and advocating for the sector since 2021. There are several associations such as Khmer Artist Association,Khmer Writers Association, Khmer Musician Association are mostly work on charity except that Khmer Writers Association provide writing workshops to aspiring writers. To develop a sector, it is understandable that policy advocacy and dialogue is strongly needed toensure the commitment from the government and it comes with knowledge and know-how from capable policy advocates like CICADA.
